title: After the Blue Tsunami: Getting rid of Trump’s tariffs
gist: Alan Wolff (PIIE) argues the new Democratic Congress (256 House, 55 Senate seats) lacks veto-proof majorities to repeal Trump's tariffs, so most tariffs face a two-year legislative stalemate with relief pinned on the courts. Realistic levers are must-pass riders like the NDAA, a narrow Canada repeal (Section 338/232), confirmation and appropriations leverage, and longer-term restoration of executive-congressional trade cooperation via fast track/TPA.

insights.claim: Alan Wolff (PIIE) expects the incoming Democratic Congress in January 2027 to face a legislative stalemate on most of Trump's tariffs for two years, leaving removal hopes pinned on the courts.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Do not price a fast legislative rollback of US tariffs before 2029; litigation is the more likely catalyst for tariff relief.
insights.quote: the likely outcome will be a legislative stalemate on most of the tariffs, leaving hopes for removing them pinned on the courts
insights.locator: Can we expect the House and Senate

insights.claim: Democrats will hold at least 256 House seats and 55 Senate seats after the 2026 midterms, short of the 290 House members and 67 senators needed to override a presidential veto of tariff repeal.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Veto-proof math is missing, so tariff repeal requires Republican defections; watch GOP cross-over votes as the signal.
insights.locator: Trump, whose term lasts into January 2029

insights.claim: Trump's probability of signing a bill lifting his tariffs is about zero because tariffs are hallmarks of his administration that he believes are correct.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Executive tariff policy should be assumed sticky through January 2029 absent court rulings.
insights.quote: The likelihood of Trump signing a bill lifting the tariffs is about zero.
insights.locator: Trump, whose term lasts into January 2029

insights.claim: Historically, Congress has overridden only 112 of 2,599 presidential vetoes since 1789, underscoring how unlikely a veto override on tariffs is.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Base rate for veto overrides is ~4%, a useful prior for any anti-tariff bill odds.
insights.locator: Trump, whose term lasts into January 2029

insights.claim: Democrats could attach a blanket repeal of Trump's tariffs to a must-pass bill like the National Defense Authorization Act, which cannot effectively be vetoed.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Watch NDAA and appropriations negotiations as the realistic vehicles for tariff rollback riders.

insights.claim: A standalone anti-tariff bill, even if vetoed, could force Trump and his congressional supporters to own the tariffs' costs to consumers and small businesses ahead of 2028.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Expect messaging votes that raise political cost of tariffs without changing policy near-term.

insights.claim: Congress's leverage over the Trump administration includes Senate confirmation of senior officials and judges, appropriations, and must-pass bills, but must be used selectively because tariffs compete with other policy priorities.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Tariff concessions could emerge as trading stock in confirmation or budget deals; monitor such linkages.
insights.quote: Members of the incoming Congress have more than tariff reform on their wish lists of policies and measures, and they will have to use their leverage selectively.
insights.locator: However, Congress does have some leverage.

insights.claim: Proposals to condition tariff authorities or require congressional agreement before the president imposes tariffs would all be veto bait if effective; the White House might accept only low-impact technical changes.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Treat any tariff-reform bill Trump signs as likely economically immaterial.
insights.quote: All of these would be Trump veto bait if effective.

insights.claim: A narrower strategy is to repeal Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the no-longer-in-force statute underpinning Trump's latest anti-Canada tariffs, but those tariffs cover only about $20 billion of US imports.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A Canada-only win would be symbolically meaningful but macro-small; don't extrapolate to broad tariff relief.

insights.claim: Trump's tariffs target a large share of total US goods imports, which are on track to reach $3.8 trillion to $3.9 trillion in 2026 by Wolff's Census-based estimate.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Scale of tariffed base dwarfs any piecemeal repeal, keeping the inflation impulse largely intact.

insights.claim: Section 232 national-security tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminum, lumber, copper, and auto parts are more damaging to Canada; US duties on Canadian imports jumped to about $10 billion in 2025 from $0.4 billion in 2024, covering about 15% of $56 billion-worth of imports by value.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Canadian metals, lumber and auto-parts exporters remain exposed; a congressional Canada exemption from 232 would be the key upside catalyst.

themes.theme: China tariffs and broad reform hurdles

insights.claim: A general tariff rollback could rationalize China tariffs by excluding goods that are net benefits to the US economy, potentially winning farm-belt votes if China fully reopens to US agricultural exports.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: US ag exporters are the swing constituency; any China-tariff deal tied to farm access would be bullish for them.
insights.locator: During both the Trump and Biden administrations

insights.claim: A China-focused tariff relief bill is not at all likely to win a veto override because appearing weak on China is politically costly, though Congress should test bipartisan support.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: China tariffs are the stickiest part of the US tariff regime; don't expect legislative relief.
insights.quote: Would a China-focused bill get enough votes to override a veto? Not at all likely
insights.locator: During both the Trump and Biden administrations

insights.claim: Banning use of trade statutes for economic coercion against allies faces three problems: defining allies is contentious, it would end Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and protected vested interests would oppose it.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Section 301 is likely to survive as a tariff tool regardless of party control.
insights.locator: Can a broader anti-tariff bill pass

insights.claim: Almost 50% of AP Voter Poll respondents said the cost of living was crucial to their congressional vote, and Wolff argues the tariffs fed inflation, creating a midterm mandate for change.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Affordability politics keep tariff rollback pressure alive into 2028; tariff-driven inflation remains a policy lever to watch.
insights.quote: The tariffs fed inflation, making life in this country less affordable.

insights.claim: Trade Promotion Authority (fast track), in place from 1975 to 2021, traded congressional delay and amendment powers for negotiation mandates and consultation; neither Trump nor Biden sought renewal after it expired in July 2021.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: No TPA means no new comprehensive US trade agreements are likely; a future president may revive interbranch cooperation.

insights.claim: Even Trump needed Congress to implement USMCA, suggesting the next president of either party may rediscover the value of working with Congress on trade.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Post-2029 trade policy could shift toward congressional partnership, relevant for USMCA review and North American supply chains.
insights.quote: The next president, whether Democrat or Republican, could discover the merits of working with Congress on trade.
